25717-the-history-of-the-decline-and-fal:
Edward Gibbon's History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire appears here in a complete contents edition, with notes by the Reverend H. H. Milman. The work was written in 1782 and revised in 1845, and this text rests on Project Gutenberg files 731 to 736 in utf eight.

David Reed, who made the Gutenberg sets, aimed to give scholars and the general public the best text possible, thanking helpers including Dale R. Fredrickson, who hand entered material. A 1996 edition carries all Gibbon's footnotes, while a 1997 edition first lacked footnotes in five volumes. This complete edition joins the whole history in order.
3073-pioneers-of-the-old-southwest-a-chr:
Constance Lindsay Skinner wrote Pioneers of the Old Southwest, volume eighteen of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. The subtitle calls Kentucky the dark and bloody ground. Skinner founds her narrative largely on original sources, the writings of pioneers such as Doddridge and Adair and public documents in the Colonial Records and American Archives. The story includes Daniel Boone's party and a night attack by Shawnee warriors spying on the camp, slaughtering sleepers barely three miles from the main camp.

Only a slave and a laborer escape to bring gloomy tidings an hour later. Terror takes hold of the little settlement. The book gives a vivid history of the trans-Appalachian frontier, grounded in documents.
32515-the-maner-of-the-tryumphe-of-caley:
The Maner of the Tryumphe of Caleys and Bulleyn, edited by Edmund Goldsmid and privately printed in Edinburgh in 1884, reprints two extremely rare Tudor tracts. The first, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1532 to 1533, describes the triumph at Calais and Boulogne. The second describes the noble triumphant coronation of Queen Anne, wife of Henry VIII. The edition was limited to seventy-five large paper copies and two hundred and seventy-five small paper copies for subscribers.

Goldsmid criticises an earlier reprint by Arber in the English Garner. Arber modernised spelling and inserted or inverted words to suit editorial taste. He misread French names such as Grammont, Tonnerre, and Montmorency. His edition preserves old spelling and names. Readers get rare primary texts on Henry VIII's court, ceremony, and Anglo-French display.
35634-the-word-hoosier-john-finley-india:
The Word Hoosier is a study by Jacob Piatt Dunn, printed at Indianapolis in 1907. It stands as volume four, number two, of the Indiana Historical Society Publications. Bobbs-Merrill issued it, together with a sketch of John Finley by his daughter Sarah Wrigley. Dunn asks where Indiana's nickname came from.

For about seventy-five years the state and its people have borne the name Hoosier, he notes. Discussion of its origin has been large, but no result satisfies. Meredith Nicholson's account, the latest and fullest, concludes the origin is not known with certainty. Dunn argues the theorists began from some false assumption of fact. He picks through their testimony like a lawyer, looking for the wrong scent.
45630-bird-guide-land-birds-east-of-the-:
Chester Reed wrote a field guide to the land birds found east of the Rockies, running from parrots to bluebirds. Reed had served as curator in ornithology at the Worcester Natural History Society and had written on the eggs of North American birds. The guide aims to help ordinary readers know the birds around their homes.

Reed opens by arguing that native birds rank among the nation's most valued assets, since they eat vast numbers of insects that harm trees and crops. He urges readers to protect birds and to draw them near their homes. The guide then treats bird after bird in order, so readers can name what they see and learn its habits. The book suits new bird watchers who want a plain, handy guide to eastern land birds.
45815-the-great-pestilence-a-d-1348-9-no:
The Great Pestilence is a history of the Black Death by Francis Aidan Gasquet. Simpkin Marshall published it in London in 1893. Its full title dates the pestilence to 1348 and 1349. The contents open with the commencement of the epidemic. First reports of the sickness and the eastern accounts come first. The great trade routes between Asia and Europe are traced. The plague in the Crimea and the siege of Caffa follow.

The origin of the name Black Death is taken up in that chapter. Symptoms of the disease are described from the sources. Constantinople's attack is told from the emperor Cantacuzene's account. Genoese traders carried the infection to Sicily, the heads note. A second chapter follows the epidemic through Italy in detail. Boccaccio's Florence and Petrarch's letter appear among the witnesses. Gasquet writes as a historian mining chronicle evidence.
48553-emblematic-illumination-or-forms-c:
Emblematic Illumination gives forms, colors, and emblems fit for painting texts of Holy Scripture in large style, in oils or watercolors. The book was gathered and edited in London by an editor who signs with initials only, and sold for five shillings and sixpence. Lithographers to the Queen printed the volume.

The preface says most handbooks treat only tiny missal painting, while most amateurs paint large scrolls. Such painters, lost on church color rules, pick hues by taste and spoil the emblem sense of their work. The book explains what each color means and which sacred symbols can be worked into a scroll with ease. Its aim is apt, rule-bound ornament over mere pretty effect.
50088-the-marryers-a-history-gathered-fr:
The Marryers is a satirical novel by Irving Bacheller. Harper and Brothers published it in New York and London in 1914. Its subtitle calls it a history gathered from a brief. The brief's author is the Honorable Socrates Potter of Pointview, Connecticut. Potter addresses his preface to the judges of decency and good behavior worldwide. His novelist friend, he says, prevailed on him to write against feudal tendencies in America.

Potter has just returned from Italy, the land of love and song. Love there, he reports, has ceased to be art and become an industry. The titolati devote hereditary talent to marrying money. Juliets now descend from the balcony to the bobsled and the tango. Most are English and American girls down from Saint Moritz. The first chapter presents the dilemma of Whitfield Norris, multimillionaire. Potter pledges enough truth for conscience, but not enough to stagger the unaccustomed.
57273-the-stocking-knitter-s-manual-a-ha:
The Stocking Knitter's Manual is a handy book for the work-table, holding patterns for knitted stockings and like work. The writer, in a note kept with the text, says the patterns were first gathered for a friend who had pupils. The friend found them of service and a saving of time in teaching others. The writer then laid them before the public in hope of wider use.

The front pages carry the publisher's list of half-crown volumes, a sign of the book's cheap, useful place in the home. Such manuals gave teachers and mothers tested patterns to work from, at a time when stockings were still knit by hand in many houses.
58058-the-royal-exchange-and-the-palace-:
Royal Exchange and the Palace of Industry is a religious tract by Thomas Binney. The Religious Tract Society of London issued it in eighteen fifty one. Its subtitle promises the possible future of Europe and the world. Psalm twenty four, The earth is the Lord, stands as its text.

Binney builds his argument in three parts on that psalm foundation text. The Royal Exchange stands for trade and the Palace for industry in his plan. The Crystal Palace year made industry a pulpit theme across Britain then. Clean hands and a pure heart mark those who ascend, the psalm says. Binney reads commerce and making as fields of Christian duty and hope.
65830-two-christmas-stories-sam-franklin:
Hesba Stretton, the much read author of Jessica's First Prayer, gathers two Christmas stories in this small volume of eighteen seventy six. Henry King and Company published it in London. Both tales belong to her specialty, the moral story of working class life. Such books were sold cheaply and read in cottages and Sunday schools.

The first story follows Sam Franklin, an artisan who marries and finds his wages stretch further than they did in his bachelor days. Cookshops and public houses no longer drain his pocket. He puzzles over a spare half crown that keeps growing, and the savings bank of the title is his slow answer. The second story, A Miserable Christmas and a Happy New Year, works the same ground from the side of a holiday gone wrong. Stretton writes plainly about rent and housekeeping money.
67691-pharmacographia-a-history-of-the-p:
Pharmacographia is a past of the chief plant drugs by Fluckiger and Hanbury. Its full name bounds the work to Great Britain and British India. A Macmillan house brought out this second print in eighteen seventy nine. The name means a writ on drugs, its front words state at once. That word was chose as clear, brief, and known in many tongues.

The book holds the pair own probes plus best finds of drug men world wide. Drug craft and cure use are left out of its plan by set choice. Plant lore and chem lore books bear those parts in the trade scheme. Points left dim get full talk where most past hands gave less. Paths for more probe are marked where the pair saw gaps in lore.
68687-lives-of-alchemystical-philosopher:
Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers is a set of lives of the old alchemists, edited by Arthur Edward Waite and published in London in 1888. It rests on materials gathered in 1815, updated by newer research. The 1815 book it rebuilds has been credited by some collectors to Francis Barrett, author of The Magus. Waite also wrote The Real History of the Rosicrucians.

The work adds a proof of the true principles of the Magnum Opus, the great work of alchemical rebirth. It also gives an account of spiritual chemistry, the inner reading of the alchemists' art. A bibliography of alchemy and hermetic thought closes the volume. The book serves students of the occult history of Europe.
69390-aristocracy-in-america-from-the-sk:
Aristocracy in America is the first volume of a work from the sketch-book of a German nobleman. It was edited by Francis J. Grund, the author of a work on the Americans in their moral, social, and political relations. The book came out in London in 1839 from Richard Bentley, in two volumes. A portrait of Martin Van Buren, President of the United States, stands at its front.

A line from Hamlet stands on the title page, against the flattery of the poor by the great. The work is dedicated to the American people. The pages were written, the dedication says, by one of their fe— as the text breaks off. The book is a foreign noble's view of rank and society in the young republic, set down for English readers of its day.
70232-aristocracy-in-america-from-the-sk:
A German nobleman's sketch book of America, edited by Francis Grund, fills this second of two volumes issued in London in 1839. A plate of President Martin Van Buren fronts the book. Grund had written on the Americans in their moral, social, and state relations, and this work keeps that theme.

Part two treats a short stay in Boston and Philadelphia. Chapters weigh the shut doors of Boston high life, the links between rich and poor in a land of equals, and the thrift of the home grown rich. North and South are set side by side. Later talk turns to the cross quizzing of foreign guests, the high worth set on common sense, and a dislike of genius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-knabl:
Joseph Knabl was a Tyrolean master of religious sculpture in wood. Born at Fliess in 1819 to poor parents, he was apprenticed to a woodcarver at Imst and studied old German carving at Munich. He taught at a trade school, joined the Mayer art institute in 1859, and in 1863 took the Munich Academy's chair of church sculpture.

His chief work, the Coronation of the Virgin in Munich's Frauenkirche, sets a larger-than-life Mary on the high altar amid angels and saints. Knabl's manner was original and deeply pious without sentimentality, recalling Overbeck and Führich. Most of his statues stand in Bavarian churches, with others at Stuttgart and Mergentheim.
doe-osti-2998012-design-of-a-system-inte:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/38, by Roberto Ponciroli, Haoyu Wang, Richard Vilim, and co-authors, designs a shared steam interface for two advanced reactors. A factory buying nuclear steam needs heat delivered steadily even as reactors age or throttle. The study picks an industrial process fit for nuclear-grade steam and ranks interface layouts that blend both reactors' output.

Scoring uses thermal efficiency, a heat factor, and surviving capacity when parts degrade. One modeled layout posts net electric output of 154.8 megawatts with thermal efficiency 0.27 and heat factor 2.99, against weaker options at 109.4 and 38.7 megawatts. Heat pumps in the layouts draw between about 84 and 258 megawatts in the cases shown. Cross-flow between system parts is modeled from pressure gaps born of temperature gaps. Plant designers get a ranked shortlist with numbers attached.
doe-osti-2999088-melcor-deposition-model:
Matthew Christian, Troy Haskin and David Luxat of Sandia National Laboratories add noble metal deposition models to a reactor safety code, in report SAND2025-12380, printed September 2025. In a liquid-fuelled molten salt reactor, the fuel salt itself circulates through the core. Noble metals, chemically quiet elements born in fission, form particles that ride the loop and settle on surfaces. Tellurium among them decays into iodine, a health hazard, so where they land shapes the accident source term.

Three deposition models went into the MELCOR code: one for turbulent fluid deposition, one for heat-driven particle drift, and one for gravity settling. Their mass transfer values were checked against records from the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment. Deposition proved strongly tied to salt flow and thickness, and to how fast particles diffuse and how big they are. The results set up the fiscal 2026 work that follows.
doe-osti-3015900-massachusetts-and-new-e:
Kristi Moriarty, Ling Tao, Anelia Milbrandt, and Gui Zheng of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this January 2026 study, NLR/TP-5400-97669, on sustainable aviation fuel in Massachusetts and New England. Sustainable aviation fuel is jet fuel made from wastes or plants instead of oil. The study maps the regional jet fuel market, current fuel plants, and the feedstocks the region could supply.

Inside, the team weighs production routes, including e-fuel made with electricity, and estimates how much fuel sites near regional airports could make. One result puts the highest output at 40.2 million gasoline-gallon equivalents near the airport coded BAF, using yellow grease, animal fats, and brown grease. Feedstock supply turned out to move cost more than any other factor. Airport and state planners can use the numbers to judge which sites deserve a closer look.
doe-osti-3367698-advanced-facility-desig:
Argonne National Laboratory final report for ARPA-E award DE-AR0001606 covers October 2023 to December 2025 work on recycling fast reactor fuel securely and economically. Amber Polke prepared it for principal investigator Nathaniel Hoyt. Recycling spent fuel recovers uranium and plutonium, but the plant must prove material cannot be diverted. The project paired advanced facility design with machine-learning safeguards from the start.

Argonne's AMPYRE flowsheet software was updated for the Oklo reactor's fuel cycle. It now outputs what a sensor placement analysis needs. A partner took it over, building a real-time digital twin of the process. Design documents and plan approvals gate each activity in the report's milestone tables. The premise is safeguards by design: instrument the plant on paper, before concrete makes changes expensive.
nasa-tm-19650015746-auxiliary-estimating:
J David Lifsey, in the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at Marshall, wrote this May 21, 1965 memorandum on a statistics problem. Sometimes a sample is cut off at both ends, so values beyond set limits never appear. Such a sample is called doubly truncated. Lifsey deals with samples drawn from a normal, bell-shaped population.

His topic is auxiliary estimating functions, extra tools that help find the best estimate from such cut data. Curves and tables support the method. Maximum likelihood estimation is the goal, in the language of the report. Workers with incomplete test data were the intended users of this careful, narrow study.
nasa-tm-19700030512-a-solar-x-ray-astron:
Robert M. Wilson, John M. Reynolds, and Stanley A. Fields of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this summary in January 1970. It covers solar X-ray astronomy, the study of X rays given off by the Sun. A long bibliography of the field fills most of the book.

The work adds an author index and a subject index to the list of sources. An appendix tabulates the flight experiments that gathered the data. Tables cover rocket and balloon flights and satellite flights alike. One table lists the solar spectral lines each flight observed. For researchers, the book was a map of a young field and its evidence.
pioneers-of-the-old-southwest-a-chronicl:
Constance Lindsay Skinner wrote Pioneers of the Old Southwest in 1919 as Volume 18 of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press. Its subtitle calls the region a chronicle of the dark and bloody ground. That was the contested frontier country beyond the early settlements.

Skinner says her narrative rests largely on original sources. These include the writings and journals of pioneers and early observers such as Doddridge and Adair. They also include public documents in the Colonial Records and American Archives. Early chapters cover the tread of pioneers, folkways, and the trader. The book records how backcountry people lived, traded, and fought as the frontier pushed west. It also names the other historians whose research she used.
